newsitem.title: USA: U.S. reviewing nursing homes inspection policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. reviewing nursing homes inspection policy.

text.p: The Clinton administration killed a controversial plan Tuesday to curtail inspection of nursing homes that care for Medicare and Medicaid patients after a consumer group and an organisation for the elderly warned it could hurt care.

"It's not going anywhere anytime soon," said Peter Garrett, a spokesman for the federal Health Care Financing Administration. "Our number one concern is the quality of care our beneficiaries receive."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said President Clinton would not allow changes that could harm senior citizens.

"He's not going to do anything, approve anything, that would put at risk those elderly living in nursing homes that need to be properly supervised, whose care needs to be properly monitored," McCurry told reporters.
Administration officials appeared determined to quickly contain any political fallout from the proposal, publicly denouncing it after it surfaced in Tuesday's New York Times.
Federal studies show two-thirds of U.S. nursing homes do not fully meet federal guidelines. That statistic includes both serious and minor violations.
The proposed changes would have narrowed the scope of inspections, limited medical records examined and ended routine review of patient admission contracts and accident reports.
Investigators would not have had to review medications in some nursing homes that performed well in a first-round survey. The number of patient interviews would have dropped.
To receive Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement, nursing homes must meet federal health and safety regulations. The federal government contracts with states for inspections.

The proposal would have altered a manual states use when inspecting nursing homes. Garrett said the changes, first proposed in October, were designed to target limited resources on the most troubled nursing homes.
He said Health Secretary Donna Shalala and other top officials had not seen the plan.

"No explanation has been given as to how these changes will help residents improve quality of life and care or assure residents, families and all citizens that the system is working," the National Citizens' Coalition for Nursing Home Reform said in a letter to the Department.
"The reviews conducted ... are becoming so narrow in scope that surveyors will virtually be going through facilities wearing blinders," the group said.
An official with the American Association of Retired Persons said he was surprised to see the proposal after the White House fought congressional efforts last year to repeal many federal standards.
As part of an unsuccessful plan to give states control of the Medicaid programme for the poor, elderly and disabled, Republicans wanted to roll back some nursing home standards.

"We are very concerned that some of the proposed changes would make it increasingly difficult to ascertain accurately which facilites, were, in fact, performing poorly," the AARP said in a letter to the Health Care Financing Administration.

The 1987 nursing home rules are credited with improving quality of life for elderly and disabled patients by reducing use of restraints, overmedication to control patients and abuse in nursing homes. More than 1.6 million people receive care in U.S. nursing homes.
